crypto.title: Cryptography Track
crypto.subtitle: 25 Levels — A Practical Cryptography Investigation
crypto.description: Work through 25 real cryptographic challenges across 5 phases: foundations, symmetric cryptography, public-key cryptography, key exchange & modern crypto, and a final investigation phase — culminating in a full incident that ties every technique together.

level01.title: Level 01: Encoding vs Encryption
level01.learn: Encoding (like Base64) transforms data into a different, transportable format — but with NO key and NO secrecy. Anyone can reverse it instantly. Encryption requires a key, and without it the data is computationally infeasible to recover.

objectives.label:
Given this string:
SGVsbG8gQ3J5cHRv

Which encoding is this? Enter the name.

Decode it:
SGVsbG8gQ3J5cHRv

Enter the exact decoded text.
Final: does Base64 provide confidentiality — i.e. does it hide the data from anyone who sees it? Enter YES or NO.

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level02.title: Level 02: Caesar Cipher
level02.mission: The simplest possible cipher — and why it's broken.
level02.learn: A Caesar cipher shifts every letter by a fixed amount. Its entire security rests on that one shift value staying secret — but with only 25 possible shifts, brute force breaks it instantly.

objectives.label:
Ciphertext:
KHOOR FUBSWR

This was encrypted with a Caesar cipher — a shift between 1 and 25. Find the shift, then enter it as a number.
Final: using that shift, decrypt "KHOOR FUBSWR" and enter the plaintext exactly.
objectives.cmd: python3 -c "print(''.join(chr((ord(c)-65-3)%26+65) if c.isupper() else c for c in 'KHOOR FUBSWR'))"

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level03.title: Level 03: Vigenere Cipher
level03.mission: A repeating key beats a single shift — but not by enough.
level03.learn: Vigenere applies a DIFFERENT Caesar shift to each letter, cycling through a keyword — the bridge between classical and modern cryptography.

objectives.label:
Plaintext: ATTACKATDAWN
Key: LEMON

Encrypt using the Vigenere cipher (each letter shifts by the corresponding key letter, A=0). Enter the ciphertext in uppercase.
objectives.cmd: python3 -c "key='LEMON'; text='ATTACKATDAWN'; print(''.join(chr((ord(c)-65+ord(key[i%len(key)])-65)%26+65) for i,c in enumerate(text)))"

objectives.label:
Final: decrypt this Vigenere ciphertext using keyword 'LEMON':
LXFOPVEFRNHR

Enter the recovered plaintext.
objectives.cmd: python3 -c "key='LEMON'; text='LXFOPVEFRNHR'; print(''.join(chr((ord(c)-65-(ord(key[i%len(key)])-65))%26+65) for i,c in enumerate(text)))"

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level04.title: Level 04: XOR / Bitwise Crypto
level04.mission: The building block of most modern stream ciphers.
level04.learn: XOR is its own inverse: (P XOR K) XOR K always gives back P. Dangerous if a key is ever reused: K = P XOR C recovers the key from any known plaintext/ciphertext pair.

objectives.label:
Plaintext byte: 0x5A
Key: 0x1F

Calculate plaintext XOR key. Enter as hex (e.g. 45).
Now reverse it: ciphertext 0x45, key 0x1F. Recover the original byte (hex).
Final: you know a plaintext/ciphertext pair — plaintext 0x7A, ciphertext 0x2C — but not the key. Recover the key using K = P XOR C. Enter as hex.

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level05.title: Level 05: Classical Cryptanalysis
level05.mission: No hints this time — investigate first.
level05.learn: Real cryptanalysis starts with recognizing WHICH cipher you're facing before you can break it. This level gave no cipher name and no shift — both had to be deduced.

objectives.label:
Intercepted ciphertext (mechanism unknown):
EPNSNZCA DPNFCTEJ EPLX NZYQTCXPO

Investigate. This is a classical substitution cipher on the alphabet — identify what kind of cipher it is. Enter 'caesar' or 'vigenere'.
Find the shift used (try each of the 25 possibilities). Enter the shift as a number.
Final: decrypt the full ciphertext and enter the recovered plaintext exactly.
objectives.cmd: python3 -c "print(''.join(chr((ord(c)-65-11)%26+65) if c.isupper() else c for c in 'EPNSNZCA DPNFCTEJ EPLX NZYQTCXPO'))"

level06.title: Level 06: AES Encryption
level06.mission: A real block cipher, not a toy.
level06.learn: Plaintext + Key, run through many rounds of substitution and permutation, produces ciphertext that reveals nothing about the plaintext without the key.

objectives.label:
AES-128-ECB key (hex): 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f
Plaintext: "TECHCORPSECURE1X" (16 bytes)

Encrypt it with openssl and enter the resulting ciphertext as hex.

Final: same key (000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f), new ciphertext (hex): 93304f88a9d1db4287d83ca955bfa364954f64f2e4e86e9eee82d20216684899

Decrypt it with openssl and enter the recovered plaintext exactly.

level07.title: Level 07: Block Cipher Modes
level07.mission: Why ECB is the mode everyone warns you about.
level07.learn: ECB encrypts each block independently, so identical plaintext blocks always produce identical ciphertext blocks — leaking structure. CBC's chaining fixes this.

objectives.label:
Same 32-byte plaintext (two identical 16-byte blocks) was encrypted twice with the same key, once per mode:

ECB ciphertext: b2fff73c73cae69350ffb919d10838b4b2fff73c73cae69350ffb919d10838b46d00049adfc582b051c393cb8678ad17
CBC ciphertext:  67196a55fd101f8c4b896fc5faf2f64dfa5372a54a4a69eb6bcf0b49eb0fb0ec6b8ec4e1f14309e6f67ae47716c8d585

One of these has two identical halves (first 16 bytes == second 16 bytes). Which MODE produced that ciphertext — ECB or CBC?
Final: why does this matter for real data (e.g. an encrypted image or a repeating record format)? Enter 'patterns' if ECB leaks patterns in the plaintext structure, or 'random' if it doesn't.

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.

level08.title: Level 08: Hash Functions
level08.mission: One-way digests and the avalanche effect.
level08.learn: A hash function is one-way: no key, no way to reverse it. Changing even one character produces a completely different, unrelated-looking digest.

objectives.label:
Message:
"Transfer Rs.5000 to account 1042"

Calculate its SHA-256 digest.

Modified message:
"Transfer Rs.9000 to account 1042"

(Only the amount changed.) Calculate ITS SHA-256 digest.
Final: comparing the two digests you just calculated, has the message been modified? Enter YES or NO.

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level09.title: Level 09: Password Hashing
level09.mission: Why passwords need a slow KDF, not a fast hash.
level09.learn: PBKDF2/bcrypt/Argon2 deliberately slow down hashing so that an attacker with a stolen hash database can only try a limited number of guesses per second.

objectives.label:
A login system stores this PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 hash for a user:
6c31d00d67b45e37cbee7e016ed4d8de8ee167df117fe603f38e055f9ea82816

Salt: 5b1e8f0a
Iterations: 100000

Candidate passwords: Summer2024!, TechCorp#99, Winter2024!

Compute PBKDF2 for each candidate and find the one that matches the stored hash. Enter the matching password.
Final: why is a slow KDF like PBKDF2 used for passwords instead of a single fast SHA-256 call? Enter 'slow' if the deliberate slowness is the defense, or 'fast' if speed is the defense.

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level10.title: Level 10: HMAC
level10.mission: Prove a message wasn't just hashed — it was hashed WITH a secret.
level10.learn: HMAC mixes a secret key into a hash so only someone who knows the key can produce a valid MAC for a given message — proving both integrity and authenticity.

objectives.label:
Message: "Transfer 1000 INR"
Secret: "crypto-training-key"

Generate the HMAC-SHA256 of the message using this secret.
objectives.cmd: python3 -c "import hmac,hashlib; print(hmac.new(b'crypto-training-key', b'Transfer 1000 INR', hashlib.sha256).hexdigest())"

objectives.label: Final: a modified message arrives: "Transfer 9000 INR" claiming the SAME HMAC (c7227054a756159571052c6e9bf5341684657affa03ac0d14a284396383768a2). Compute the real HMAC of this modified message and compare — does the original HMAC still verify? Enter VALID or INVALID.
objectives.cmd: python3 -c "import hmac,hashlib; print(hmac.new(b'crypto-training-key', b'Transfer 9000 INR', hashlib.sha256).hexdigest())"

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level11.title: Level 11: RSA Mathematics
level11.mission: Construct a real RSA keypair step by step.
level11.learn: An RSA keypair starts with two secret primes p and q. n=pq is public; phi(n)=(p-1)(q-1) must stay secret; d is the modular inverse of e mod phi(n) — the private key.

objectives.label: The two primes for this RSA keypair aren't given directly — they were recovered from a decommissioned server's leftover files. Investigate /home/student/evidence in the terminal to find them, then calculate n = p x q. Enter n.

Using the same two primes you found:

Formula:
phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1)

Enter phi(n).

Given:
e = 17
phi(n) = 3120

Find d such that:
e x d = 1 (mod phi(n))

Enter d.

Your RSA keypair is now:
Public key (n, e) = (3233, 17)
Private key (n, d) = (3233, 2753)

Which one must never be shared — n, e, or d? Enter one letter/value.

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level12.title: Level 12: RSA Encryption
level12.mission: Encrypt a message with a public key.
level12.learn: RSA encryption is one formula: c = m^e mod n, using the PUBLIC key. Anyone can do this step.

objectives.label:
Public key:
n = 3233
e = 17

Plaintext:
m = 65

Formula:
c = m^e mod n

Enter the ciphertext c.

level13.title: Level 13: RSA Decryption

Ciphertext:
c = 2790

level14.title: Level 14: RSA Key Recovery
level14.mission: Given only n, e, and a ciphertext — break it yourself.
level14.learn: If an attacker can factor n back into p and q, they can rebuild phi(n) and then d — fully breaking the encryption. This is why real RSA uses enormous primes.

objectives.label:
You are given only:
n = 3233
e = 17
ciphertext = 538

No p or q this time — but a decommissioned server's evidence files are mounted at /home/student/evidence. Search them (ls, find, cat, grep, strings) to recover the two prime factors. Enter them as p,q in ascending order, e.g. 5,11.
Using p=61, q=53: calculate phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1). Enter it.
Using e=17, phi(n)=3120: find d such that e x d = 1 (mod phi(n)). Enter d.

Final: decrypt the ciphertext from the start of this level.
c = 538, n = 3233, d = 2753

m = c^d mod n

Enter m.

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level15.title: Level 15: RSA Signatures
level15.mission: Sign with a private key, verify with a public key.
level15.learn: A signature is RSA run in reverse: sign with your PRIVATE key, verify with your PUBLIC key. Tampering with the signed data breaks verification.

objectives.label:
Using the keypair from Level 11 (n=3233, d=2753), sign a message's hash-digest stand-in h=15:

signature = h^d mod n

Enter the signature.

Verify it with the PUBLIC key (n=3233, e=17):

check = signature^e mod n
signature = 452

Enter 'check'. It should match the original digest h=15.

The file is now modified. Its digest is 22 instead of 15, but the attacker kept the SAME signature (452).

Verify the same signature again. Does it still check out against the NEW digest? Enter VALID or INVALID.

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level16.title: Level 16: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange
level16.mission: Two sides derive one shared secret, in public.
level16.learn: Each side publishes g^private mod p, then combines the OTHER side's public value with their OWN private value. Both land on the identical shared secret without ever transmitting it.

objectives.label:
Public values (agreed openly):
p = 23
g = 5

Alice's private value: a = 6

Formula:
A = g^a mod p

Enter Alice's public value A.

Bob's private value: b = 15

Formula:
B = g^b mod p

Enter Bob's public value B.

Alice computes the shared secret from Bob's public value:
S = B^a mod p
B=19, a=6, p=23

Enter S.

Final: Bob computes the shared secret from Alice's public value:
S = A^b mod p
A=8, b=15, p=23

Enter S — it should match Alice's result.

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level17.title: Level 17: Diffie-Hellman MITM
level17.mission: Why unauthenticated key exchange isn't enough.
level17.learn: Standard DH authenticates nothing about who sent a public value — an active attacker can substitute their own values and establish separate shared secrets with each victim.

objectives.label:
TechCorp's network log captured a Diffie-Hellman exchange between Alice and Bob (p=23, g=5):

Alice sent public value: 8
Bob received public value: 4
Bob sent public value: 19
Alice received public value: 4

Alice and Bob each received the SAME public value instead of each other's. What is that shared attacker value?

Final: standard Diffie-Hellman authenticates nothing about WHO sent a public value — only that it's a valid number mod p. Does unauthenticated DH prevent this man-in-the-middle attack? Enter YES or NO.

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level18.title: Level 18: Elliptic Curve Cryptography
level18.mission: Point addition, doubling, and scalar multiplication.
level18.learn: Elliptic curve points form a group under a geometric addition rule. Scalar multiplication is easy forward, and hard to reverse — the elliptic-curve discrete log problem.

objectives.label:
Curve: y^2 = x^3 + 2x + 2 (mod 17)

Is the point (5, 2) on this curve? Check both sides of the equation. Enter YES or NO.
Base point G = (5, 1) IS on the curve. Compute point doubling: 2G = G + G, using the elliptic-curve group law. Enter the result as 'x,y'.
Final: compute scalar multiplication 6G (i.e. G added to itself 6 times) using double-and-add. Enter the result as 'x,y'.

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level19.title: Level 19: ECDH
level19.mission: Diffie-Hellman, but on an elliptic curve.
level19.learn: Same idea as classic DH, but public values are curve points and the combining operation is scalar multiplication instead of modular exponentiation.

objectives.label:
Same curve, base point G = (5, 1).

Alice's private scalar: a = 4

Compute Alice's public point: A = a*G. Enter as 'x,y'.

Bob's private scalar: b = 3

Compute Bob's public point: B = b*G. Enter as 'x,y'.
Alice computes the shared point: S = a*B, using B=(10, 6) and a=4. Enter as 'x,y'.
Final: Bob computes the shared point: S = b*A, using A=(3, 1) and b=3. Enter as 'x,y' — it should match Alice's result.

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level20.title: Level 20: Digital Signatures — Software Update
level20.mission: Detect a tampered update before installing it.
level20.learn: Verifying a software update's signature before installing it is exactly how systems catch backdoored or corrupted updates before they run.

objectives.label:
TechCorp published update.bin (contents: "techcorp-agent-v4.2.1-release-build") with a digital signature (1199), using the Level 11 keypair (n=3233, e=17, d=2753).

The signature was produced over a digest stand-in derived from the file's SHA-256 hash.

Verify it: check = signature^e mod n, signature = 1199. Enter 'check'.

A second copy of update.bin arrives, contents now:
"techcorp-agent-v4.2.1-release-build-BACKDOORED"

claiming the SAME signature (1199). Its digest stand-in is now 250 instead of 581.

Final: does the original signature still authenticate this file? Enter VALID or INVALID.

Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level21.title: Level 21: PKI & Certificates
level21.learn: A certificate's Subject and Issuer fields reveal whether it was vouched for by a trusted third party, or only by itself.

Now check who signed (vouched for) this certificate — its Issuer CN. Enter it.

Final: the Subject CN and Issuer CN are identical — this certificate signed itself, rather than being signed by a trusted Certificate Authority. Is this certificate trustworthy for a production service that other companies connect to? Enter YES or NO.

level22.title: Level 22: Key Derivation Functions
level22.mission: Turn a password into a usable encryption key.
level22.learn: A KDF (like PBKDF2) turns a low-entropy password into a fixed-length key suitable for use in a symmetric cipher.

objectives.label:
Password: "R3set-2026-kdf"
Salt: 9c3fa61d
Algorithm: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256
Iterations: 50000
Key length: 16 bytes

Derive the key and enter it as hex.
objectives.cmd: python3 -c "import hashlib; print(hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', b'R3set-2026-kdf', b'9c3fa61d', 50000, dklen=16).hex())"

objectives.label: Final: use the derived key (as raw bytes) to XOR-encrypt the message "PIVOT-OK" (repeating-key XOR against the key bytes). Enter the result as hex.
objectives.cmd: python3 -c "import hashlib; k=hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', b'R3set-2026-kdf', b'9c3fa61d', 50000, dklen=16); m=b'PIVOT-OK'; print(bytes(b^k[i%len(k)] for i,b in enumerate(m)).hex())"

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level23.title: Level 23: CSPRNG vs Predictable Randomness
level23.learn: A cryptographic key is only as strong as the randomness that generated it. An LCG's output is fully predictable from its formula; a real CSPRNG's is not.

objectives.label:
Two random-number generators produced these 5-value sequences:

Generator A: [27, 264, 753, 806, 735]
Generator B: [812, 47, 963, 205, 588]

Generator A uses this known formula: x_next = (1103515245 * x_prev + 12345) mod 2^31, output = x_next mod 1000, seeded with x_0=42.

Using that formula, predict the NEXT value Generator A will produce.
Final: which generator is UNSAFE for producing cryptographic keys or nonces — 'A' or 'B'?

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level24.title: Level 24: Cryptanalysis Investigation
level24.mission: Unlabeled ciphertext — you decide the approach.
level24.learn: No cipher name given. Recognizing single-byte XOR from its structure, then brute-forcing all 256 keys, is the entire challenge.

objectives.label:
Evidence file /home/student/evidence/ciphertext.bin contains this hex-encoded data:
7662737e631a6365767e7b1a747b7276791a00070305

You are NOT told which cryptographic mechanism produced it. Investigate: what is the shortest possible key length that could produce readable English when XORed against this data? Enter the length in bytes (a number).

Brute-force all 256 possible single-byte keys against the ciphertext and find the one key that produces readable, all-uppercase text (letters, digits, hyphens only). Enter the key as a two-digit hex value (e.g. 1f).
objectives.cmd:
python3 -c "import string
allowed=set(string.ascii_uppercase+string.digits+'-')
c=bytes.fromhex('7662737e631a6365767e7b1a747b7276791a00070305')
for k in range(256):
 d=bytes(b^k for b in c)
 if all(32<=x<127 for x in d) and set(d.decode()) <= allowed: print(f'{k:02x}')"

objectives.label: Final: using that key, recover and enter the full plaintext exactly.
objectives.cmd: python3 -c "c=bytes.fromhex('7662737e631a6365767e7b1a747b7276791a00070305'); print(bytes(b^55 for b in c).decode())"

hints: Hint 1: Work through the formula/steps given, using the exact values provided.
Hint 2: Use the terminal as a calculator (python3, sha256sum, openssl, xxd) — don't try to do large modular exponentiation by hand.

level25.title: Level 25: Final Cryptographic Incident
level25.mission: Verify, decrypt, and close a real case.
level25.learn: Real incident response verifies authenticity and integrity BEFORE trusting decrypted data enough to act on it. This case chains encoding, XOR, hashing, and RSA signatures together.

TechCorp's security team received an encrypted communication from an unverified server. The evidence bundle is at /home/student/evidence/crypto-incident/. Start by reading README.txt, then inspect encrypted_message.bin (hex) and server_config.txt (which contains the XOR key used, hidden among other config lines).

encrypted_message.bin (hex): 797f1f6e797f786c7e467b5e7f417c7e7e1a527d787f7b5e657e4150677b1717

objectives.cmd: python3 -c "c=bytes.fromhex('797f1f6e797f786c7e467b5e7f417c7e7e1a527d787f7b5e657e4150677b1717'); print(bytes(b^42 for b in c).decode())"

Base64-decode that string:
SU5DSURFTlQtUkVTT0xWRUQtOTkzMQ==

Final: the incident is fully verified. Submit the recovered case record, wrapped as FLAG{...}.
